content: To produce a comprehensive guideline document of 5000 words, it is highly recommended to avoid a committee approach to writing. While it may seem cost-effective to request experts to draft chapters for free, this method often results in challenges related to quality, consistency, and timely delivery, ultimately creating more work than it eliminates. When referencing proprietary products, it is essential to avoid naming specific brands. Devices and diagnostics used in interventions should be described generically, without identifying specific products or trademarks. If there is any uncertainty, consult the World Health Organization’s (WHO) legal counsel for guidance. Editing and proofreading are critical steps in the guideline development process. WHO Press maintains a list of approved freelance editors and proofreaders, along with sample terms of reference and standard pay rates. It is important to note that the best editors and proofreaders are often booked months in advance, so production schedules should be planned early, and their time reserved accordingly. The final guideline document must undergo executive clearance and Guidelines Review Committee (GRC) approval. This review occurs as part of the final executive clearance process. Documents submitted for clearance should be in their final, edited form, ready for layout and printing. Once the text has been edited, proofread, and cleared, it must be sent for layout. WHO Press can provide advice on external typesetters and the specifications required for contracting this work. Additionally, the WHO graphics team offers an internal layout service. Design decisions should be carefully considered, as they can significantly impact production, printing, dissemination, and translation costs. Using an existing publication template from WHO Press may help reduce costs. A cover design, an International Standard Book Number (ISBN), and a barcode are also required, with the latter two issued by WHO Press. For printing, internal print services will provide quotes and arrange for the files to be sent to the printer. It is essential to have the printer’s proofs checked by the proofreader, so this step should be included in the initial proofreading contract. Once the printed copies are delivered, the focus can shift to distribution and implementation. Disseminating guidelines involves making them accessible, advertising their availability, and distributing them widely. Guideline developers should consult WHO Press regarding priced and mandatory free distribution. Dissemination options include online publication, where a web-ready PDF (optimized for easy download and navigation) is the minimum requirement. Depending on the guideline’s length and audience, full-text HTML and additional materials (both electronic and printed) may also be considered. The WHO web team can provide valuable advice in this area. Translations may be necessary to reach a global audience, particularly in the six official languages of Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian, and Spanish. Translation efforts must be planned in advance, with timing discussed with suppliers or regional offices. Budgeting for translation costs is essential, and to reduce expenses, translations may be limited to executive summaries. Systematic reviews commissioned for the guideline may be submitted for publication in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization or other journals. Cochrane reviews are published in the Cochrane database. To increase awareness of the guideline, its process and recommendations may also be published in peer-reviewed journals. Other dissemination methods include mobile phone applications for guideline dissemination and decision support. Developers may also consider planning an official launch, issuing a press release or holding a press conference, making an announcement on the WHO website, distributing through regional offices or meetings, or seeking endorsement from stakeholders and interest groups. Guidelines should include a review-by date to indicate how long the recommendations are expected to remain valid. The validity period depends on the pace of research advancements, areas lacking evidence, and the potential need for new advice. For standard and full guidelines, a minimum of two years and a maximum of five years is suggested. The department responsible for initiating the review should be named in the document. Updating recommendations can be challenging, especially if evidence must be retrieved to support numerous existing recommendations. Priority should be given to controversial areas or those with new evidence. Interim updates may be necessary if new evidence supports or contradicts current recommendations. Such updates should be based on a new or updated systematic review and reviewed by the GRC if they involve changes to recommendations. Updates that add new evidence without altering recommendations do not require review, although GRC review may be advisable for highly controversial topics or evidence. Implementation of a guideline should be considered from the beginning of its development. Ideally, the project should be part of a departmental or programmatic work plan on the topic, as this increases the likelihood of effective implementation. Implementation is generally the responsibility of regional, national, or subnational groups, which is why their involvement in guideline development is crucial. WHO headquarters and regional offices can support implementation by providing tools, support, and coordination. Implementation strategies should be tailored to local circumstances. Basic steps include analyzing local needs and priorities, identifying barriers and facilitating factors, determining available resources, and designing an implementation strategy. Derivative documents or tools, such as slide sets, manuals, flow charts, decision aids, fact sheets, quality indicators, checklists, and templates, can facilitate implementation. These materials can be distributed with the guideline or developed by local implementers. Operational research can inform field testing and rollout strategies to promote the adoption of recommendations. Impact assessments should be conducted in the locations where the guidelines are implemented. WHO should collaborate with Member States to evaluate the guidelines’ impact by coordinating efforts and providing advice and practical support. For further reading, several resources are available, including works by Grol, Wensing, Eccles, and others, which provide insights into improving patient care, implementing evidence-based practices, and evaluating the effectiveness of clinical practice guidelines.
